slides.title: From Dots to Digits
slides.kicker: You once added 5 plus 7 with dots!
bullets: As beginners we added by drawing dots: 5 dots for 5, 7 more for 7, then counted all 12 dots.
Imagine adding 473 and 695 by drawing dots; the page would fill up before we finished.
Luckily we discovered a much faster way to add, hidden inside the Indian number system.

left.title: Counting dots
items: Count every dot one by one

right.title: Column addition
items: Write numbers one below the other
Add each column right to left
Carry when a sum is 10 or more

slides.note: Dots are sweet for 5 plus 7, and pure torture for 473 plus 695.

slides.title: Align Digits Right
slides.kicker: The Indian place-value system makes it work.
bullets: Write the numbers one below the other, with the rightmost digit aligned.
In the base-ten place-value system, the rightmost column is the ones place.
Right alignment makes ones meet ones and tens meet tens, so columns can be added one by one.
slides.note: Ones first, boss: right to left is the rule.

slides.title: The Carry Rule
slides.kicker: Ten or more? Pass one to the left.
bullets: Add the digits of a column. If the sum is 10 or more, write only the units digit below the column.
Set the value of carry to 1, and add that carry in the next column on the left.
If the column sum is less than 10, write the sum directly and set carry to 0.

items: Sum is 10 or more: write units digit
Add carry in the next column

slides.note: Carry is always 0 or 1, never more.

slides.title: Repeat, Then Finish
slides.kicker: Move left until no digits remain.
bullets: Move to the next column on the left and add the two digits plus the current value of carry.
Repeat this until there are no more digits on the left.
If the final carry is 1, write it to the left of the bottom row of the answer.

slides.title: What Is an Algorithm?
bullets: Our addition method is an algorithm: a step-by-step procedure to arrive at an answer.
We describe an algorithm by writing down the steps as precisely as possible.
Follow the steps exactly; do not perform any action that is not explicitly mentioned.

slides.title: When Numbers Differ in Size
bullets: Exercise 11.1 asks what happens when a 5-digit number is added to a 3-digit number.
In the base-ten place-value system an empty column simply counts as 0, so the steps still work.
It also asks why carry cannot exceed 1: the biggest column sum is 9 plus 9 plus 1, which is 19.
slides.note: Exercises are gym time for your algorithm.

slides.title: gcd From Scratch
slides.kicker: Forget prime factorisation; use the definition.
bullets: Computing the greatest common divisor, or hcf, is a familiar problem.
We have already solved it using prime factorisation and other methods.
Now we solve it straight from the definition of gcd, as a written algorithm.
slides.note: Old tools aside, today we argue from the definition.

slides.title: Break the Problem Down
bullets: The first step is to understand what is required and break the problem into smaller pieces.
We want the gcd, so first we compute the divisors of both numbers and note them down.
Then we compare the two collections and find the largest number present in both.

slides.title: Hunt for Divisors
slides.kicker: Check every j from 1 up to n.
bullets: To compute gcd(375, 825), start by finding the divisors of 375.
Any divisor, or factor, of 375 must lie between 1 and 375.
The simplest way is to check each number between 1 and 375 and see if it divides 375.

slides.title: Keep a List
bullets: We must keep track of the divisors so we can compare them with the divisors of 825.
Maintain them in a sequence, or a list, written with square brackets like [1, 4, 9, 16].
The list starts empty, and every time we find a new divisor we add it at the end.
slides.note: New divisor joins at the end, queue style.

slides.title: The Divisor Algorithm
bullets: Step 1: start with an empty list-of-divisors.
Step 2: for each number j in the sequence 1, 2, 3 up to n, if j divides n, add j to the list-of-divisors.
Names like list-of-divisors and j keep the description precise; without j it would be clumsy.
slides.note: Give things names, yaani labels, and steps stay crisp.

slides.title: Executing an Algorithm
slides.kicker: Run the steps on a real number.
bullets: Running through an algorithm step by step is called executing the algorithm.
Execute it on 18: j = 1, 2 and 3 divide 18; j = 4 and 5 do not; j = 6 does.
The finished list is [1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 18], the divisors of 18 in ascending order.
slides.note: Watch it run: 1, 2, 3 in; 4 and 5 out.

slides.title: Names Carry Values
bullets: Executing an algorithm computes intermediate quantities, like the lists divisors-of-m and divisors-of-n.
We give each value a name so we can refer to it later in the algorithm.
Assigning names to intermediate values is what keeps the written algorithm concise.
slides.note: carry was a named value too, back in 11.1.

slides.title: A List Is a Data Structure
bullets: Intermediate values are typically more complicated than simple numbers.
Here we maintain lists of numbers, arranged in ascending order.
A list is an example of a data structure.
slides.note: A list: a shelf with a system.

slides.title: Organise to Go Fast
bullets: Data structures organise information in a manner that makes an algorithm more efficient.
In an ascending list, the largest divisor found so far always sits at the end.
This idea opens a big field of study that we will explore in higher grades.

slides.title: One Scan Instead of Two
slides.kicker: m plus n checks shrink to max(m, n).
bullets: Scanning 1 to m for divisors of m, then 1 to n for divisors of n, checks m + n candidates.
Let max(m, n) be the maximum of m and n, and run a single scan of j from 1 to max(m, n).
If j divides m, add it to the divisors of m; if j divides n, add it to the divisors of n.
The number of possible divisors to check drops from m + n to max(m, n).

right.title: One combined scan
items: Run j from 1 to max(m, n)
Test j against m and n

slides.title: Common Divisors Direct
slides.kicker: Why keep two lists? Keep one.
bullets: With the scans combined, we can directly compute the list of common divisors.
Instead of building both divisor lists and combining them, record j only when it divides both.
The common divisors come out in ascending order, so the last one is the largest, the gcd.

items: Run j from 1 to max(m, n)
Does j divide both m and n
If yes, add to common list

slides.title: Think Like a Designer
bullets: Exercise Set 11.2 asks for algorithms to find elements of one list that are missing from another.
It also asks for an lcm algorithm, and whether writing divisors in pairs, like (2, 9) for 18, speeds up the scan.
Improving the steps without changing the answer is the heart of algorithm design.
slides.note: Same answer, less work: that is elegance.

flashcards.back: A step-by-step procedure to arrive at an answer, with every step written as precisely as possible.

flashcards.front: In column addition, when does the carry become 1?
flashcards.back: When a column sum is 10 or more: write the units digit below the column and pass carry 1 to the left.

flashcards.front: Why are the digits aligned from right to left?
flashcards.back: Right alignment lines up ones with ones and tens with tens in the Indian place-value system, so each column adds matching places.

flashcards.front: Why can the carry never be more than 1?
flashcards.back: The largest column sum is 9 plus 9 plus 1, which is 19, still below 20, so the carry is only ever 1.

flashcards.front: What does the gcd of two numbers mean?
flashcards.back: The greatest common divisor, or hcf, is the largest number present in both collections of divisors.

flashcards.front: State the algorithm to find all divisors of n.
flashcards.back: Start with an empty list-of-divisors; for each j from 1 to n, if j divides n, add j to the list-of-divisors.

flashcards.front: What does executing an algorithm mean?
flashcards.back: Running through the algorithm step by step, doing exactly what each step says and nothing more.

flashcards.front: How does the book write a list of values?
flashcards.back: Inside square brackets, like [1, 4, 9, 16], with every new divisor added at the end of the list.
A way of organising information, such as a list, that helps make an algorithm more efficient.

flashcards.front: Why do we name intermediate values like divisors-of-m?
flashcards.back: Named values can be referred to later in the algorithm, which keeps the written steps concise.

flashcards.front: One combined scan checks max(m, n) candidates instead of what?
flashcards.back: Instead of m plus n, the total of scanning 1 to m and then 1 to n separately.

flashcards.front: How do the divisors of 18 pair up?
flashcards.back: As (1, 18), (2, 9) and (3, 6): each small divisor pairs with 18 divided by that divisor.

quiz.q: To add 473 and 695 with the digit-by-digit algorithm, which digits do you add first?
options: All the digits together at once
quiz.why: Step 2 of the algorithm starts at the rightmost column and later steps move left.

quiz.q: A column sum is 10 or more. What do you write directly below that column?
options: The units digit of the sum
The tens digit of the sum
quiz.why: The book says write the units digit below and set the value of carry to 1.

quiz.q: A column has digits 8 and 7, and carry 1 arrives from the right. What is written below, and the new carry?
quiz.why: 8 plus 7 plus 1 is 16, so the units digit 6 goes below and carry becomes 1.

quiz.q: Adding 473 and 695 gives 1168. Where does the leftmost 1 of the answer come from?
options: From the carry left after the last column
quiz.why: Step 5 says if carry is 1 at the end, write it to the left of the bottom row.

quiz.q: Any divisor of 375 must lie between which two numbers?
quiz.why: A divisor, or factor, of a number lies between 1 and the number itself.

quiz.q: When the divisor algorithm begins, what does list-of-divisors hold?
options: It holds every number up to n
quiz.why: Step 1 starts with an empty list; each new divisor is added at the end.

quiz.q: Executing the divisor algorithm on 18, which is the first candidate j that fails the test?
quiz.why: 1, 2 and 3 all divide 18, but 4 does not, so 4 fails first.

quiz.q: For gcd(375, 825), how many candidate divisors do the two separate scans check in total?
quiz.why: We scan 1 to 375 and then 1 to 825, and 375 plus 825 is 1200.

quiz.q: The lists of divisors we build are arranged in which order?
quiz.why: Section 11.3 maintains lists of numbers arranged in ascending order.

quiz.q: With one combined scan for m = 375 and n = 825, how many candidates get checked?
quiz.why: The scan runs from 1 to max(375, 825), which is 825, instead of 1200.

quiz.q: In the direct common-divisor scan, j is added to the list only when...
options: It divides m but not n
It divides both m and n
It divides neither m nor n
quiz.why: Common divisors must divide both numbers, so j is recorded only then.

quiz.q: Divisors of 18 pair as (1, 18), (2, 9), (3, 6). Roughly where can a paired scan stop?
quiz.why: Past sqrt(n) every pair has already appeared, so checking near 4 suffices.

examples.title: Run the addition algorithm on 473 plus 695
examples.problem: Use the digit-by-digit addition algorithm from Section 11.1 to add 473 and 695. Follow each written step precisely and do not perform any action that is not mentioned.
steps: Step 1: write the numbers one below the other in the base-ten place-value system, digits aligned from right to left: 473 on top, 695 below it.
Step 2, rightmost column: 3 plus 5 is 8, which is less than 10, so write 8 below and set the value of carry to 0.
Step 3, middle column: 7 plus 9 plus carry 0 is 16, which is 10 or more, so write the units digit 6 below and set carry to 1.
Step 3 again, leftmost column: 4 plus 6 plus carry 1 is 11, which is 10 or more, so write 1 below and set carry to 1.
Step 4: there are no more digits on the left, so stop repeating.
Step 5: the value of carry is 1, so write 1 to the left of the bottom row.

examples.title: Execute the divisor algorithm on 18
examples.problem: Execute the algorithm to find the divisors of n for n = 18, showing how the list-of-divisors grows, and write the final list in the book's square bracket notation.
steps: Step 1: start with an empty list-of-divisors.
Try j = 1: 1 divides 18, so add it at the end; the list becomes [1].
Try j = 2 and j = 3: both divide 18, so the list grows to [1, 2] and then [1, 2, 3].
Try j = 4 and j = 5: neither divides 18, so nothing is added.
Try j = 6, then j = 9, then j = 18: each divides 18, so the list grows to [1, 2, 3, 6], then [1, 2, 3, 6, 9], then [1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 18]. Every other j from 7 to 17 fails the test.

examples.title: gcd(375, 825) by the improved scan
examples.problem: Compute gcd(375, 825) by directly computing the list of common divisors with one combined scan, and state how many candidates were checked compared with the two-scan method.
steps: The two scans of 1 to 375 and 1 to 825 can become one scan of j from 1 to max(375, 825), which is 825.
Keep j only if it divides both 375 and 825. Testing each j this way, the common divisors are 1, 3, 5, 15, 25 and 75.
The list of common divisors in ascending order is [1, 3, 5, 15, 25, 75].
The largest number present in both collections of divisors is the last entry of this ascending list.
The combined scan checked 825 candidates, while two separate scans would have checked 375 plus 825, which is 1200.
examples.answer: gcd(375, 825) is 75, found by checking 825 candidates instead of 1200.

flowchart.title: How an algorithm gets built and improved

steps.label: Meet a problem
steps.detail: Add two numbers, or find the gcd of two numbers.

steps.label: Break it down
steps.detail: Split the problem into smaller pieces we know how to solve.

steps.label: Write precise steps
steps.detail: Describe the method as exact steps, like the addition algorithm.

steps.label: Name the values
steps.detail: Give names such as j, carry and list-of-divisors to intermediate values.

steps.label: Execute step by step
steps.detail: Run the algorithm on real inputs like 18 or 473 plus 695.

steps.label: Check odd cases
steps.detail: Try a 5-digit plus 3-digit sum and confirm the steps survive.

steps.label: Improve the scan
steps.detail: Combine two scans into one, from m + n checks down to max(m, n).

steps.label: Organise with structures
steps.detail: Keep results in ascending lists so the algorithm runs efficiently.
